newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - New U.S. town seeks to restore glory of bygone age.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New U.S. town seeks to restore glory of bygone age.

text.p: Any American of a certain age has an image of this place -- a small town where the houses have white picket fences and chairs on the porch, where decency, trust and the family reign supreme.

The image of small town America, immortalised in the paintings of Norman Rockwell, is decades old. But it still has a powerful attraction in an increasingly isolated and rootless society that has been torn by crime, violence and cynicism.

Now, on a plot of former swampland in Florida, the business empire that gave the world Mickey Mouse is trying to resurrect the kind of community that Americans once took for granted and which they now fear may be vanishing altogether.
The town of Celebration, built from scratch by the Disney Corporation in the last few years, is a place where the sun shines all the time -- provided you have the money.

"We liked the idea of having an old-fashioned neighbourhood like we used to have years ago," said Roger Burton, a private investigator from Chicago who was among the first residents to move here in June.
Sitting on the broad, fenced porch of their home with their Old English sheepdog, Burton and his wife Cathy explained how the town's cosy atmosphere attracted them and their two children.
"People have the same values and priorities....it's the people that have chosen to live here that I enjoy the most," said Cathy.
"That's the way it was in the 50s and 60s, you had a neighbourhood where...you would know everyone on your street. Now you don't, now you're lucky if you know your next-door neighbour," said Roger.
Celebration has a small downtown area next to a lake, a school, a bank, a post office, shops, a cinema, parks, nature trails and a golf course. A fitness centre and hospital will open next year.

Everything is within easy walking distance and the spacious houses have been built in a style that deliberately echoes the world of the 1940s and 1950s, with big windows, white fences and green mailboxes.
The town roads have names like Honeysuckle Avenue and Sycamore Street. A lone policeman watches traffic from beneath a fluttering Stars and Stripes in the park, as children leave school for the day.
People are relentlessly pleasant and cheerful and vices such as smoking or swearing are not in evidence. Everything is clean and neat.
It is a million miles from the strip malls, anonymous suburbia and highways that cover much of the United States.
But if you're searching for exciting nightlife or a vibrant ethnic mix, look elsewhere.
Disney, which has been planning the project for almost 10 years, has tried to promote the town as a multi-cultural community but the overwhelming majority of the residents are white and affluent.
House prices start at around $130,000 and rise to around $1 million -- far out of reach for many who would like to escape the problems and pressures of urban America and make a fresh start.
About 400 residents, chosen by lottery because demand was so high, have moved in since the first houses were completed in June.

Builders are busily finishing off other dwellings in time for the official "Founders' Day" celebrations in mid-November, to the irritation of some residents who are annoyed by the constant noise and the trucks rumbling past their new homes.
Over the next decade or so, Disney plans more development and hopes Celebration will grow into a thriving town of around 20,000 people.

Those who come to live here can choose from six styles of architecture for their new home and, to discourage property speculators, must forfeit any profits if they sell up and leave within three years.

Disney, which built the town just a few miles (km) from its famous Walt Disney World resort outside Orlando, denies suggestions that it is creating a controlled environment, a kind of Orwellian nightmare town where everyone will have to conform.
Mickey Mouse and his cartoon cohorts from the Magic Kingdom, where all endings are happy endings, are nowhere to be seen.

"A community builds over time and establishes its own culture," said Don Killoren, vice-president and general manager of Celebration. "We've not tried to tell them what their values should be...We ensure the community is run properly, that operations are tight...It's a very profitable venture for us."
John Armstrong, a 68-year-old Briton who has lived in the United States for the last 30 years, moved here in June with his wife.
He said claims that Disney is controlling people's lives were "absolute rubbish", although he acknowledged that the cost of living in Celebration would not make it available for everyone.
"It is a little expensive for some people," he said.
The company refuses to say how much it has invested to date in Celebration, although some reports have put the figure at more than $2 billion.

There has also been an effort to combine the best of new technology with the world of small town America. Fibre optic links, a computer network for the town and the latest in health care are all on offer behind the old-fashioned facades.
"Everything we do is also very modern," said Killoren. "It really is an integration of the best ideas of small town planning of previous years and the best ideas of today."
